articles.title_orig: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.title_zh: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.
The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.
It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.
Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.
Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening .
I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.
I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.
But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.
I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.
For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.
One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.
I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.
Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.
This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.
While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.
I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.
I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.
Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.
These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.
Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.

articles.title_orig: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.title_zh: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats.
This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton.
After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny.
In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead.
Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country:
Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening.
"Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote.
"This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued.
Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024.
Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development.
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post.
Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX.
In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state.
Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
"I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added.
Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC.
"I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer."
"I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out."
Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election.
Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami."
It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing.
While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted.
Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman.
Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami.
Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections.
In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown."
But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade."
Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds.
The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July.
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout.
"I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
Ahead of the midterms, some in tech expressed concern that Democratic wins would mean additional scrutiny on data centers, which have faced fierce opposition in communities across the US.
Dan Ives, a veteran Wall Street analyst and AI bull, said the midterms will put the brakes on the rapid construction of data centers.
In a post on X, he said the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years."
Ives added that while some investors will prefer a slower pace, others will view it as added risk.
"We estimate 10% of data centers will not happen now," he said.
Richard Branson, the billionaire founder of the Virgin Group, wrote in a post on LinkedIn that the results of the midterm election are not just "a decisive repudiation of Trump" but also an encouraging sign "about the limits of money in politics."
Branson wrote, "As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on — mostly Republican — campaigns this election cycle, in an attempt to buy influence and control over public policy."
Branson added that voters looked past the "hateful and false messages" fueled by the billions spent on funding candidates, voting based on the issues that mattered to them.
"I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform," he wrote.

Based on the details, at around 11:30 that evening, indicators of unusual potential activity by Hamas leadership were detected, but a different and reassuring explanation was estimated for what was happening.
At around 12:00 midnight, an intelligence officer in the southern command informed the commander that it was possible that the senior Hamas official, Mohammed Deif, would descend into a tunnel designated as an emergency site.
During a conversation between them, several potential assessments were raised, including fears of an Israeli military operation, or training, or the more serious possibility of a surprise preemptive operation.
At 01:46 AM, the then Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi was updated by the office of the head of the General Security Service (Shabak) on the developments.
This was the first conversation that night reaching the Chief of Staff's office regarding developments in the Gaza area.
The Shabak requested to focus on Mohammed Deif's movements and gather more information.
At 02:30 AM, information was received indicating that in a certain area of the sector, rocket launch sites began to activate, and as a result, a series of conversations started to update senior officers with the information, including Halevi and the head of operations, along with the southern region commander.
Based on those developments, Halevi conducted a situation assessment, where he decided that although there was no logic for a preemptive offensive operation, the information should be examined very cautiously in order to fully understand Hamas's intentions and what might surprise us, as he stated at that time.

articles.title_orig: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products are compromised
articles.title_zh: Cyberattack hits French blood bank site but no blood products are compromised
articles.content_orig:
Europe’s refrigeration hacks hit healthcare: France’s EFS confirms an attack on blood plasma storage, with no products lost.
Published on November 4, 2026
© Aman Chaturvedi - Unsplash
I am Laio, the AI-powered news editor at IO+. Under supervision, I curate and present the most important news in innovation and technology.
France’s national blood service, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS), confirmed a cyberattack on November 1 that disrupted refrigeration systems storing blood plasma and platelets. Hackers remotely altered temperature settings in three cold storage sites, pushing levels from -30°C to as high as 110°C.
Technicians intervened before any products were compromised, but the incident underscores the vulnerability of critical healthcare infrastructure to cyber-physical threats. The attack is part of a coordinated wave targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, including supermarkets in at least 11 countries.
Over the past weeks, hackers have targeted refrigeration systems in supermarkets across Europe, causing temperatures to spike to 50°C in stores in Belgium, Sweden, Ireland , and eight other countries. In October, Dutch retailer Albert Heijn was hit by an attack that shut down its websites, delivery services, and parts of its store operations.  The U.S. military also reported suspected cyberattacks on commissary refrigeration systems in August. Authorities suspect state-sponsored actors or lone-wolf hackers, though no group has claimed responsibility.
The cyberattacks leveraged flaws in refrigeration controllers. These vulnerabilities allowed hackers to bypass authentication using a hidden daily password and execute remote commands to manipulate temperature settings.
In the EFS case, the attackers targeted systems supplied by Coolworld, forcing freezers to defrost and risking the spoilage of blood plasma, which must be stored below -25°C. The French cybersecurity agency CERT-FR had previously warned about these vulnerabilities, urging organizations to remove public internet access and restore remote access via secure VPNs. Despite these alerts, over 2,765 Danfoss refrigeration systems remained exposed to the internet.
The EFS acted quickly to mitigate the impact, with its technicians promptly detecting the anomaly and transfering blood products to other facilities, preventing any damage. The agency also reinforced temperature monitoring and alerted France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the health ministry.
Meanwhile, EU officials convened an emergency meeting of the interinstitutional Task Force, involving ENISA and Europol, to coordinate a response. National authorities in Italy, Belgium, and Sweden launched investigations, with some treating the incidents as deliberate attempts to disrupt critical supply chains. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that AI-powered malware could exacerbate such threats in the coming years.
This attack highlights once more the systemic vulnerabilities of the so-called operational technology (OT) systems, often overlooked in cybersecurity strategies.  Many refrigeration controllers lack basic protections, such as strong authentication or network segmentation, making them easy targets for remote manipulation.
The incidents have forced retailers and healthcare providers to reassess their OT security posture, with experts recommending Zero Trust segmentation, inline enforcement, and multicloud visibility. The EU’s NIS2 Directive and DORA framework now require stricter cybersecurity measures for critical infrastructure, but compliance remains inconsistent. The financial and operational fallout from these attacks underscores the need for urgent action.

articles.title_orig: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.title_zh: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.
For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.
Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?
Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:
Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.
Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”
After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.
“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.
Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.
The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.
Top Republicans blame Iran war for midterm results
“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”
Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.
Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.
In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.
Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.
“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”
Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.
“We are at the end of an era,” he said.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.
The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.
Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.
Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.
For Kyiv, the reaction came before the election. And on Wednesday there was relative silence.
For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.
And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.
A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.
But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.
There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.
There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. The Eufy Window Cam E10 sticks directly to the inside of a window so installation takes less than a minute.﻿
The Eufy Window Cam E10 sticks directly to the inside of a window so installation takes less than a minute.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Anker announced a new indoor security camera that’s designed to watch your yard, driveway, or front porch through a window, instead of monitoring what’s inside your home. The new Anker Eufy Window Camera E10 takes a similar approach to the Wyze Window Cam that launched nearly a year ago . It installs right against a window using an including mounting sticker to reduce glare and reflections, but the camera doesn’t require any weatherproofing since it’s not enduring the elements outdoors.
The Eufy Window Camera E10 is available now for $79.99 through Anker’s online store and Amazon , making it more than twice as expensive as the $34.98 Wyze Window Cam . But the E10 comes with a few useful upgrades. Wyze’s camera is limited to 1080p, while the E10 has a much higher maximum resolution of 2.5K, capturing more detailed 15fps videos at 2,688 x 1,520.
The E10 also offers a slightly wider and taller field of view than Wyze’s camera at 105 degrees horizontal and 57 degrees vertical. But to accommodate a wider range of installations such as an upstairs window the angle of the E10’s camera can be manually adjusted up and down by 25 degrees using a wheel on the back to ensure the areas you want monitored are properly in frame.
Other features of the E10 include color night vision, AI-powered motion detection and alerts that can differentiate between humans, animals, and vehicles, and a microphone that’s limited to louder noises given the camera’s location. Footage can be recorded locally to a microSD card up to 256GB in size, or pushed to the cloud with an optional subscription. And while Anker claims installation can take less than a minute, you will have to deal with potentially routing and hiding a power cord since the E10 lacks a rechargeable battery.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine falls behind Moldova on path to EU membership
articles.title_zh: Ukraine falls behind Moldova on path to EU membership
articles.content_orig:
President Volodymyr Zelensky in Berlin, Germany, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Florian Gaertner / Photothek via Getty Images)
The EU is championing Ukraine's future membership louder than ever, but its Nov. 4 annual report on the state of Kyiv's integration process makes clear that the country must get serious about the rule of law.
In this year's annual reports on the progress of EU candidate countries towards membership , Ukraine was singled out by the European Commission as a "frontrunner," along with Moldova, Montenegro, and Albania, leapfrogging long-time candidates such as Serbia.
"Ukraine has shown steadfast commitment to European integration through continued reform implementation, even in the face of (the) most difficult circumstances brought by Russia's war of aggression," reads a Commission summary of the report.
The Commission is pitching Ukraine's "potential" to the bloc in "critical raw materials, energy, agriculture, digital technologies, and defense production," and stresses that the country is "already contributing" to the EU's defense readiness and response to hybrid threats.
And on digitalization, the Commission's report calls Ukraine "a global frontrunner."
But while the Commission says it is committed to supporting Ukraine's "ambitious" objective of closing accession negotiations by the end of 2028, it also says "that to meet it, an acceleration of the pace of reforms is required."
Ukraine expects to open the final two of the six so-called enlargement clusters in December 2026.
The clusters are lists of reforms across 33 chapters that Kyiv must carry out to align with the bloc. Once the talks are complete, a treaty of accession can be drafted.
But before Ukraine closes all chapters, it will have to get sign-off on some rule of law reforms, classified as "interim benchmarks."
And unfortunately for Ukraine, the 109-page report contains repeated criticisms, namely regarding the lack of progress on the rule of law and anti-corruption efforts.
"Limited progress" was made on the rule of law roadmap, according to the document.
And the December 2025 10-point reform plan , spearheaded by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos and then-Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Taras Kachka, "remains mostly outstanding."
"No laws were adopted to significantly advance the anti-corruption legal framework."
"Ukraine did not make progress in aligning its legislation with the EU… on the fight against serious and organized crime," the report read.
And "no laws were adopted to significantly advance the anti-corruption legal framework."
Because of that, the report repeatedly mentions the need for "urgent" reforms that Kyiv needs to adopt to meet the interim benchmarks.
Among those urgent reforms is bringing independent international experts into the process of nominating judges. The Commission describes Ukraine's "continued resistance" as a cause for "concern."
Reforming the process of appointing the Prosecutor General was also deemed urgent. The process needs to be "more transparent and merit-based," says the Commission report, as opposed to the current arrangement, in which the Prosecutor General is appointed by the president and confirmed by the parliament.
The role has been in the spotlight in recent months after the previous office holder, Ruslan Kravchenko, was dismissed amid a corruption probe and fled to Austria.
And despite Ukraine's continued climb in world press freedom rankings , the Commission stressed that further work is needed.
"Harassment and intimidation of journalists… continued to be recorded at similar levels as in previous years," notes the report.
The report also, for the third year in a row, called on Ukraine to reconsider the so-called "telethon."
Branded as "Yedyni Novyny" ("United News"), the telethon was launched at the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. It was created by merging the coverage of Ukraine's biggest TV channels.
The telethon was initially seen as a legitimate response to Russia's aggression, but later, it was accused of monopolizing television coverage and sidelining independent and opposition voices.
"In 2026, substantial public funding of around (Hr) 1.5 billion ($32.9 million)... for the telethon continued, despite declining levels of public trust and outreach," reads the Commission report.
At the same time, the public broadcaster Suspilne is still receiving "below the legal requirement" of state funding, the report notes.
Despite the significant amount of work to be done, the report shows that Brussels believes Ukraine is capable of rising to the challenge.
"Recently there has been a renewed focus in Ukraine on the reforms," the Commission notes repeatedly, echoing what EU diplomats have been telling the Kyiv Independent since Serhii Koretskyi took over as prime minister in July.
And the Commission likewise mentions its new joint task force with Ukraine. Launched in October, it aims to wrap up the rule of law reforms laid out in the interim benchmarks within around four months.
Ukraine does not have to start from scratch when it comes to closing the chapters. The report is laced with dozens of references to "good progress" and "some progress" having already been achieved.
According to an accompanying roadmap document, the Commission estimates Ukraine could close seven of the 33 chapters by the end of 2027,  based on current progress.
For some of the reforms yet to be enacted, the Commission is also trying to communicate their tangible benefits to the Ukrainian public.
One example of this is the Single European Payments Area (SEPA), which Ukraine has yet to join.
For that, Kyiv must pass anti-money-laundering legislation. In return, the Commission notes that SEPA membership "facilitates faster and less costly euro payments."
Given that the EU accounts for 65% of Ukraine's trade in goods, the benefit of joining SEPA could well be significant for Ukrainian businesses.
The Commission also cites Ukraine's joining the bloc's mobile roaming area in January 2026 as an example of how integration steps have already yielded concrete benefits.
But perhaps the strongest sign of trust is the Commission essentially telling EU countries to get ready for new member countries.
"Enlargement preparedness should become an integral part of Union policymaking," the Commission notes.
As the next step, it says EU countries "need to lead the national debate about enlargement, especially where public support and awareness are comparatively weaker."
"The Commission stands ready to support them in this effort," reads their communication.
Hi, this is Chris Powers. Thanks for reading this article. The EU is a famously complicated beast to understand, but for Ukraine, it has also never been so important.
Whether it's Russia sanctions, fighting corruption, keeping Ukraine's finances in the black, or the process of joining the EU itself, many Kyivan roads eventually pass through Brussels.
If you like reading about these fiendishly complex topics and want to support journalists in Kyiv and Brussels to shine a light on it all, please consider supporting The Kyiv Independent.
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.

articles.title_orig: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.title_zh: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.content_orig:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

articles.title_orig: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.title_zh: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.content_orig:
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has begun consultations with political parties on whom to task with forming a new coalition government, after he received the official results of a general election last week he said had no clear winner.
Herzog told party leaders that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if they want to avoid a new election.
Neither the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his rival Gadi Eisenkot secured a majority in parliament.
Earlier, electoral officials said there was no evidence of irregularities and that unsubstantiated claims by Netanyahu's camp of Arab-led parties "stealing" the election did not justify delaying the results' certification.
The Shin Bet security service is investigating allegations of foreign interference in the election, but the head of the Central Elections Committee stressed that they would not fundamentally change the outcome.
In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.
The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem.
"In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said.
"One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."
Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening.
"In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.
The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.
But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared".
"I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.
Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.
It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.
Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".
On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".
His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.
Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

articles.title_zh: How will the midterms blue wave affect my 401(k)? Answers here

SPY rose in five of six Novembers after midterms, gaining as much as 6% in 2002 and 2022 following severe bear markets.
DIA finished higher in all six post-midterm years, with gains ranging from 5% to 20%, fitting a broader presidential-cycle pattern.
In 2018, SPY gained nearly 2% in November then crashed 9% in December, ending the year 7% below pre-election levels.

Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That was up 1.16% from its November 3 close of $754.35. Reuters reported that stocks rallied and the dollar dipped after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. But one session tells a 401(k) holder very little. The more useful guide is how the index behaved in the weeks and months after past midterms. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks.
SPY's monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY's October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth.
The 2002 and 2022 cycles stand out. Both followed severe bear markets, and in each case SPY rallied after the vote. SPY rose more than 5% in November in both years. The worst case was 2010, when the index closed in November exactly where it closed in October.

The longer view is even more consistent. The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It finished higher in all six cycles since 2002, measured from the October close before each vote to the November close a year later. The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before: the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle.
For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November's gains in 2002 and 2022.
Even the 12-month periods that ended higher had real turbulence along the way. From November 2018 through October 2019, SPY returned 12.2%, yet at one point it sat 8.8% below its prior peak. From November 2022 through October 2023, SPY returned 4.2% and included an 8.3% drop. From November 2014 through October 2015, SPY returned just 2.4% and fell 8.5% between July and September 2015. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%.
This cycle starts from a higher level than most. SPY began Wednesday up 11.9% for the year and 265.9% over 10 years. Still, it went into the vote down 0.86% for the week and 0.85% for the month. The technology-packed Nasdaq-100 has been choppier. The Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) hit $762.86 in October but ended the month at $690.49, 9.5% below that peak. It closed at $685.28 on November 3.
Early sector responses point to rotation, with groups moving in different directions. The Wall Street Journal reported that defense stocks sold off after Democrats' midterm gains. A change in congressional control can reshape spending priorities, and the sectors most tied to Washington tend to adjust first, before broad index funds feel much of the shift.
Over the long run, Wall Street has tended to come out stronger after midterms. The Dow ETF's six-for-six record a year out backs that up. The shorter-term lesson from 2018 is that a strong November can turn into a rough December. I'm watching whether SPY holds above its October close of $755.72 through year-end. Falling below the pre-election October close is exactly what happened in December 2018. For index fund and 401(k) holders, the record points to a positive year ahead, with at least one sharp drop likely along the way (a drawdown early in retirement does far more damage than one later on, which is the whole subject of our free guide on defending the first five years: The First Five Years).

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla stocks sink as analyst warns Democrats' victory will create 'major hurdles' for AI build-out
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla stocks sink as analyst warns Democrats' victory will create 'major hurdles' for AI build-out
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
One of Wall Street's biggest AI bulls says the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections will slow the pace of the AI data center build-out in the US over the next two years. AI-related stocks dropped on Wednesday, including Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) and EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ), which fell 4% before trimming losses as the rest of the market surged.
Shares of cloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and data center-related companies IREN ( IREN ) and Vertiv ( VRT ) also traded lower on Wednesday after Democrats won a majority in the House and Senate on Tuesday night and flipped governorships across key states.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," Yorkville's partner and managing director, Dan Ives, wrote on Wednesday.
Those hurdles, Ives said, will slow the pace of 800 to 1,000 planned AI data centers across the US. The analyst pointed out that the biggest worry for tech investors and the AI trade is the state of Texas, where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor race over incumbent Greg Abbott in a surprise result. While Abbott currently has a moratorium on data centers in Texas, the prevailing view was that it would have ended were he reelected.
"Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors," Ives said.
This poses a problem for companies like Texas-based SpaceX, which has been building out its AI infrastructure and taking steps toward a potential merger with Tesla.
"SpaceX and Musk are clearly caught front and center in this spiderweb," said Ives.
"There will be a lot of negotiations and politics on this front especially in Texas which is the foundation of the AI buildout in the US … and Big Tech will need to embrace this new political landscape as of today," he added.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk wrote on X following the election results.
Data center concerns emerged as a key issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with candidates facing growing public opposition to proposed facility locations, the expansion of power infrastructure needed to support them, and concerns that rising electricity demand could drive up consumer costs.
One silver lining for investors may be that political headwinds will force a slowdown in AI capex. AI-related jitters have already weighed on the Tech sector ( XLK ) in recent weeks, with financing concerns hitting neocloud providers that rent out computing capacity, while semiconductor stocks have also retreated.
Long-term, however, Ives remains bullish on the AI trade, as "the Street still is way underestimating the future revenue growth and profitability" stemming from AI.
Fundstrat's Tom Lee is also largely optimistic despite the blue wave.
"President Trump exercises veto power vs any potential 'anti-AI' 'anti-data center' bills," Lee wrote in a note on Tuesday prior to the election results. He also noted that Democrats would likely embrace AI data centers because they bring money and jobs to a community.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s plans new value bundles next year after US traffic falls in third quarter
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s plans new value bundles next year after US traffic falls in third quarter
articles.content_orig:
Traffic at U.S. McDonald’s restaurants fell during the third quarter as customers struggled with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living
Traffic at U.S. McDonald’s restaurants fell during the third quarter as customers struggled with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living.
U.S. same-store sales – or sales at locations open at least a year -- fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald's since early 2025.
McDonald’s restored in-app deals and its marketing was focused on value during the quarter, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast food companies.
Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.
“This is the environment that we’re in right now. You have to be on your game and deliver that value,” said McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski during an investor presentation last month. “The pressure around cost of living isn’t going away.”
Globally, same-store sales rose 1.3% in the same period that U.S. sales fell. Strong sales in Germany and Australia helped offset weakness in France, which was rocked by protests that began in September.
Revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion for the quarter, short of Wall Street expectations of $7.28 billion.
Net income rose 9% to $2.49 billion. Adjusted for one-time items, the company earned $3.57 per share. That beat analysts’ forecast for a $3.38 per-share profit.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Bonds Hit New Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Bonds Hit New Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans.
There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia .
Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.
The City of Harwood voted against a charter rule amendment that would have required additional review before city approval of industrial developments, including data centers.
In Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers," 21 local measures were up for a vote, according to Ballotpedia.
The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue.
OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website .
SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year.
Nvidia is also backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total.
The Ohio Governor's Mansion also turned blue, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor."
Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process.
Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder.
Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot.
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030.
In one of the biggest results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, and putting the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities.
Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI, and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions of dollars this election cycle, largely came up empty.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X.
The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry as a whole.
Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Casar also accused Republicans of being "bought and paid for by AI billionaires," arguing that voters had rejected that influence and warning Democrats to "hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."
He said the data center fight is only the beginning.
"The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election," he said. "And in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics."
—CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: US Oil Inventories Fall Further As Demand Holds
articles.title_zh: US Oil Inventories Fall Further As Demand Holds
articles.content_orig:
Distillate inventories fell by 3.6 million barrels to 99.3 million barrels, while commercial crude stocks slipped by 865,000 barrels
The Energy Information Administration reported on Wednesday that U.S. distillate fuel stocks, a category covering diesel and heating oil, dropped 3.6 million barrels over the week ended Oct. 30, leaving 99.3 million barrels in storage.
That put distillate inventories at their smallest since May 2003, and 13% under the typical five-year level for this season, according to The Wall Street Journal .
Commercial crude oil stocks, not counting the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, dropped 865,000 barrels to end the week at 409.8 million barrels, the EIA said. The level was 4% below the five-year average. The decline was the fifth in a row, according to The Wall Street Journal’s count of weekly data.
Oil held in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve declined 399,000 barrels, leaving 282.2 million barrels in the stockpile. Inventories at Cushing, Oklahoma, which serves as the delivery point for U.S. crude futures, climbed 280,000 barrels and reached 27.3 million barrels.
U.S. crude output edged up 11,000 barrels a day, reaching an estimated 14 million barrels daily. Crude imports held at 6.4 million barrels a day, but U.S. exports dropped 1.2 million barrels a day, landing at 3.7 million barrels daily. Net crude imports grew 1.18 million barrels daily.
Refinery utilization climbed to 94.5%, up from 92.8% in the prior week. Crude input to refineries grew 199,000 barrels daily, reaching 16.7 million barrels daily.
Gasoline inventories shed 222,000 barrels, leaving 209 million barrels in storage, or 2% under the five-year average. Demand for gasoline climbed 450,000 barrels a day, reaching 8.8 million barrels a day.
Oil futures fell after the data. Brent crude stood at $101.30 a barrel as of 10:40 a.m. ET, a decline of $2.30. West Texas Intermediate futures lost $2.19 and were priced at $93.90 a barrel.

double quotation mark The American people have also sent a message that they are sick of Trump’s scandals, from his blatant corruption to his close friendship with Epstein and, most recently emerging from the Epstein files, an allegation of rape. Will the first secretary of state join me in saying that in this house we will not tolerate powerful men who abuse their position against women in this parliament or any other? double quotation mark The honourable lady raises an incredibly important point about the Epstein files and everything that they revealed. She’s absolutely right to highlight the importance always of challenging power and standing on behalf of vulnerable victims.
Cooper is referring to allegations contained in some of the Epstein files, recently set out at some length in a report from the Democrats on the House judiciary committee.
This is probably the first time rape allegations about Trump have been raised in the Commons.
Burghart says the Labour way is more welfare, more tax and more borrowing. They are too weak to do the right thing, he claims. Everyone else is paying the price.
double quotation mark If Labour doesn’t want to do the right thing, why doesn’t it just get out of the way?
The Speaker reprimands a Tory MP for “trying to shout a woman down”.
Haigh says Burghart, a historian, once wrote a paper titled “ Profile of a Doomed Elite”. It could have been about the shadow cabinet, she suggests.
She stresses the government’s achievements.
double quotation mark This administration has in our first 100 days [been] cutting business rates for 70,000 businesses, cutting tax for entrepreneurs, cutting VAT from electricity bills, helping 20 million households with energy bills, scrapping standing charges, capping bus fares, investing in our high streets, extending parental pay, tackling rough sleeping.
Burghart says the government won’t fix welfare. The Milburn review was delayed until after the budget. And Pat McFadden once said Labour MPs just wanted more welfare spending. So will the government commit to not putting up taxes to pay for more benefits?
Haigh says the government will bring welfare spending down, but ensuring that it now longer pays for failure. She says Burghart is on record as saying the Tories should apologise for what happened when they were in office. But Kemi Badenoch was in cabinet at the time.
Burghart says, in her comments about the budget, Haigh missed out the bits “where the Resolution Foundation said that this budget would be catastrophic for living standards” and where the OBR said tax rises could cost jobs.
He asks about the 10-year plan.
double quotation mark I’m old enough to remember Keir Starmer’s 10-year plan because it was six months ago. This is the only political party in history to have two 10-year plans in ten months.
Haigh says Burghart can ask the same question, but he will get the same answer.
Burghart says last week John Healey said in an interview he would bring welfare spending down in this parliament. This caused panic in Downing Street, he says. He goes on:
double quotation mark The prime minister was sent out to clarify things. He said the welfare bill needs to come down, but this can’t be done by cutting the welfare bill.
Then, then at teatime, the chancellor conceded defeat and said it’s not correct to say that we’re going to bring the welfare bill down.
So will the first secretary of state be clear? Why isn’t Labour going to bring the welfare down.
Haigh says Burghart was not listening to here earlier answer. And she criticises the Tories for voting against the budget last night.
double quotation mark They voted against a council tax cut for 20 million households. They voted against VAT of electricity bills. They voted against taking 70,000 small businesses out of business rates, and they voted against a tax on banks to fund it all.
Burghart says the figure is £183bn. He goes on:
double quotation mark That’s the highest figure ever. It’s higher than anything during Covid. It is higher than defence schools and policing combined. It is nearly £10,000 for every working household in this country. So will the government commit to bring that bill down in this parliament?
Haigh says the government is taking measures to bring welfare spending down.
Alex Burghart starts with a short question. How much will the government spend on working age welfare?
Haigh congratulates Burghart on his job. He has said he will correct Kemi Badenoch when she is wrong. That will make him the busiest man in Westminster, she says.
She says the government is committed to getting welfare spending down. Under the Tories, welfare spending rose by £88bn, she says.
Matthew Patrick (Lab) asks Haigh to restore the opportunities for young people that Brexit took away.
Haigh says she agrees. She says an SPS deal with the EU will help the economy, and the government is also negotiating a youth experience scheme. She says Alex Burghart has already promised to rip up these deals.

articles.title_orig: Secret police files released in Hungary, 47 years after fall of communism
articles.title_zh: Secret police files released in Hungary, 47 years after fall of communism
articles.content_orig:
The files were released on Wednesday as part of a campaign promise by Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar
Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule.
Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members.
The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution.
"I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity,"  Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest.
"Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."
Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.
How the downfall of Serbia's VuÄiÄ mirrored that of Hungary's OrbÃ¡n
Hungarian MPs scrap OrbÃ¡n's anti-LGBTQ measures
In the ensuing decades, conservative, Socialist-Liberal, and Fidesz-led governments  have all contemplated, but ultimately refused to open the files.
Since 1998, it has been possible to apply for your own file, and for historians to research those of others. But many names were blacked out, and many files withheld by the post-communist secret services for their own use.
Over the past 36 years, there were frequent leaks of data from the files, as successive governments tried to damage their opponents. Many files were also shredded, as the Communist party lost its grip in 1988-89.
From Wednesday, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services have become available on the nyitottaktak.hu website , external .
So-called Form 6 cards have been released (above) showing people's full details, but B-dossiers detailing recruitment registers will come next February
A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer.
Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.
These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided.
Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.
Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary.
Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.
Krisztian UngvÃ¡ry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power.
"In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna BorvendÃ©g, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party.
Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

articles.title_orig: ‘Like opening the Ark Of The Covenant’: Scientists crack code on treasure ship’s padlock — solving 400-year-old maritime mystery
articles.title_zh: ‘Like opening the Ark Of The Covenant’: Scientists crack code on treasure ship’s padlock — solving 400-year-old maritime mystery
articles.content_orig:
As if they found the Davey Jones’ locker combination.
Scientists used cutting-edge scanning techniques to crack the code on a shipwreck’s combination padlock that had been buried in the sand for over 400 years.
“I was blown away that we actually cracked it,” Dr David Williams, a research associate based at Cardiff University’s School of Engineering, told the BBC.
The security device belonged to the Ann Francis , a treasure-loaded vessel that sank off the coast of South Wales in December 1583 after getting caught in a fierce storm while returning from Spain.
The ship’s cargo lay untouched on Morfa Beach in Port Talbot until the late 1990s , when it was discovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes, who found a massive hoard of gold and silver coins , personal belongings, kitchen utensils, along with the aforementioned brass lock.
While the loot was recovered and donated to the Museum Wales in 2017, Hughes failed to hack the ancient safeguard after years of trying.
“I tried to unlock it for about 20 years, I tried moving the dials, finding the right combinations, and I failed,” the 69-year-old lamented, comparing the caper to the “Da Vinci Code.”
Then, recently, a collaborative team from Museum Wales and Cardiff University finally managed to decipher the gadget’s four-letter password: ANCE.
To get to the bottom of the caper, the shipwreck sleuths relied on micro-computed tomography (CT), a scanning technique normally used to examine the human body, the Independent reported. Williams said he was initially “skeptical” as the tech was “not designed for this particular purpose,” but was nonetheless “open to the challenge.”
Thankfully, by recreating a detailed 3D image of the lock’s internal mechanism, the safecracker was able to see “how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination.”
This was no mean feat given that the inside featured four rotating rings, each bearing six different letters, yielding a total of 1,296 different combinations (the ancient equivalent of encryption perhaps).
To make things more difficult, there were also letters on the ends that don’t move, suggesting they were decoys used to fool prospective looters.
Dr. Williams said that unveiling the lock of ages’ access code was immensely satisfying, gushing, “It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery.
Meanwhile, the discovery also provided closure for Hughes. “For me, it’s like opening the Ark of the Covenant, and I’m delighted, truly thrilled,” he declared.
It’s yet unclear what the padlock was protecting, but researchers speculate that it could’ve been guarding captain’s chest filled with Spanish silver, high-value textiles, or sensitive maritime documents.
For many experts, the padlock itself was the real buried treasure.
“It was in wonderful condition,” said Museum Wales’ senior curator Siân Iles. “This is a wonderful example of one that still functions as it would have done hundreds of years ago.”
He added, “Because it was found so close to the wreck of the Ann Francis and with all the material that’s part of that collection, it provides a really good context; it allows us to really tightly date it.
The cracked padlock is now on public display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.

articles.title_orig: Mother, daughter dead in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.title_zh: Mother, daughter dead in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.content_orig:
A mother and daughter have been killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack in Bella Coola.
According to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service, two individuals were reported missing by family on Nov. 1, prompting Bella Coola RCMP and rescue crews to launch a search.
On Tuesday, the service said one of the individuals was found dead in the area of the Snooka West Trail on Monday afternoon. Evidence at the site suggested an animal was involved and conservation officers were called in. The body of the second individual was found Tuesday afternoon after search efforts by conservation officers and RCMP.
Family members have identified the victims as Jenny Balcarras, 48, and daughter Selah Reed, 19.
